title: Stack & queue problem practice
overview: A practice module: you use the stack and queue built in Modules 13 and 14 to solve judge problems. The goal is to recognise when a problem is secretly a stack problem (matching, undo, most-recent-first) or a queue problem (first come, first served, rotating order). Each problem from the module's two problem sets has its own solution below: first the Problem Links list, then the Practice Day 02 list. The Module 14 folder holds earlier attempts at the same problems.

body: No new data structure today: everything you need was built in Modules 13 and 14. What this day trains is one small decision you have to make before writing a single line: **is this a stack problem or a queue problem?**

Two everyday pictures answer it. A canteen counter has a pile of washed plates. New plates go on the top, and whoever needs a plate takes the top one, the plate put down last. A ticket window has a line of people. You join at the back, and the person served next is the one who has been waiting longest.
intro.trace:
pile of plates        ticket line

  [ D ]  <- take       A  B  C  D
  [ C ]                ^        ^
  [ B ]                serve    join
  [ A ]                here     here

body: So the question to ask a problem is: when the time comes to deal with something, is it the **newest** thing that must be dealt with, or the **oldest**? Newest first means a stack. Oldest first means a queue. Nothing else about the problem matters for this choice.

**First worked example.** Check that the brackets in `( [ ] )` are balanced. You read `]`. Which opening bracket is it supposed to close? Not the first one you saw, but the most recent one still waiting, which is `[`. The last thing seen has to be dealt with first, so the waiting brackets belong on a stack.
intro.trace:
string:  ( [ ] )

read (   push        stack: (
read [   push        stack: ( [
read ]   top is [ -> pop     stack: (
read )   top is ( -> pop     stack: empty

stack empty at the end  ->  balanced

body: Notice what the stack saved you. Without it, for every closing bracket you would walk backwards through the string hunting for the nearest opening bracket that is still unmatched. That is a loop inside a loop: O(n²), which on a string of 100000 characters is about 10,000,000,000 steps and will not finish in a second. With a stack every character is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so the whole scan is O(n).

**Second worked example**, this time with arrival order. A queue holds `1 2 3 4 5` and you must reverse only the first 3. Pour those 3 through a stack, because a stack hands them back in the opposite order, then rotate the untouched 2 items from the front to the back so they end up behind again.
intro.trace:
queue: 1 2 3 4 5      k = 3

pop 3 into a stack    stack: 3 2 1  (top first)
                      queue: 4 5
push them back        queue: 4 5 3 2 1
rotate 5 - 3 = 2      queue: 5 3 2 1 4
  front to back       queue: 3 2 1 4 5

body: Three patterns cover most of the linked problems. **Matching and cancelling**: push each character, and pop instead of pushing when the new one cancels the top. Brackets work this way, and so do backspaces and removing adjacent duplicates. For `abbaca` the stack goes `a`, `ab`, then the second `b` cancels the `b`, the next `a` cancels the `a`, so `c` and `a` are pushed and `ca` is what is left.

**Next greater element**: for every number, find the first larger number to its right. Comparing every pair is O(n²). Instead walk from right to left with a stack holding only the numbers that could still be somebody's answer: pop everything not larger than the current value, and what is left on top is the answer.

**Simulation with a queue**: when the problem describes people or jobs arriving and being handled in order, act the story out. Join at the back with `push`, serve the front with `front()` and `pop()`, and send someone to the back of the line by popping and pushing the same value.
intro.snippet:
if(!st.empty() && st.top() == c) st.pop();
else st.push(c);

body: Two habits save most of the wrong answers here. Always check `empty()` before `top()`, `front()` or `pop()`, because reading the top of an empty stack is not an error message, it is undefined behaviour. And remember the stack only lets you touch the top: to reach the bottom, or to keep a running minimum, you need a second stack or a recursive call to hold the rest while you work.
The concepts below name each pattern with its snippet, and the practice links are the problems to try. Decide plates or ticket line first, and the code usually follows in a few lines.

concepts.explain: A stack only lets you touch the top. Use it when the newest item must be handled first, like the last opened bracket or the last typed character.
Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, the top must be its partner; if the stack is empty or the top does not match, the string is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty.
For problems like 'backspace' or 'remove adjacent duplicates', push characters and pop when the new character cancels the top. What is left in the stack is the final string (read it bottom to top).

Pouring a queue into a stack and back reverses it, because the stack gives items back in the opposite order. To reverse only the first k items, pour k items through a stack, then rotate the remaining n-k items to the back.

concepts.term: Inserting at the bottom of a stack
concepts.explain: You cannot reach the bottom directly. Pop everything into a helper (another stack or recursion), push the new value, then push everything back.
Keep a second stack that stores the minimum so far at every level. Push `min(x, minStack.top())` together with each push, and pop both together, so `getMin` is O(1).
A queue adds at the back and removes at the front. Use it when order of arrival matters, or to rotate items (pop from front, push to back).

files.title: Valid Parentheses with a stack
files.what: Checks that every bracket is closed by the right type in the right order. Opening brackets wait on a stack; each closing bracket must match the one on top.
steps: Walk through `s` one character `c` at a time.
An opening bracket is pushed: it now waits for its partner, and the newest one is on top.
A closing bracket with an empty stack means nothing is open to close: return `false`.
Otherwise compare it with `st.top()`: the right partner is popped, the wrong type returns `false` at once.
After the loop, `return st.empty()`: anything still on the stack was never closed.
files.input_note: The number of strings, then one bracket string per line.
files.output_note: `true false false true false`, matching LeetCode's examples. `([)]` fails at `)` because the top is `[`; `((` fails only at the end, because the stack is not empty.
files.watch_out: Calling `st.top()` on an empty stack is undefined behaviour, which is why the `st.empty()` check comes first for a string such as `)(`.

check.q: Why is a stack the right tool here and not a queue?
check.a: A closing bracket must match the most recently opened bracket that is still open, and a stack gives back the newest item first.

files.title: Backspace String Compare
files.what: Types each string into a stack (a letter is pushed, `#` pops the last letter) and then compares the two stacks.
steps: The helper `typed(s)` starts with an empty `stack<char>`.
A normal letter is pushed, as if typed on screen.
A `#` pops the top letter, but only when the stack is not empty (backspace on an empty box does nothing).
`backspaceCompare` builds both stacks and returns `typed(s) == typed(t)`; `==` on two stacks compares size and every element.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.input:
3
ab#c ad#c
ab## c#d#
a#c b
files.input_note: The number of pairs, then two strings per line.
files.output_note: `true`, `true`, `false`, matching LeetCode's examples: both of the first pair become `ac`, both of the second become empty, and the third pair ends as `c` versus `b`.
files.watch_out: Without the `!st.empty()` check, a string that starts with `#` (like `#a`) would pop an empty stack.

check.q: What does `typed("ab##")` leave in the stack?
check.a: Nothing: `a` and `b` are pushed, then each `#` pops one of them.

files.title: Insert an element at the bottom of a stack

problem.name: Code360 - Insert An Element At Its Bottom In A Given Stack

files.what: Lifts every value into a helper stack, pushes `x` onto the now-empty stack, then pours the helper back so the old values sit on top of `x` in their old order.
steps: Pop everything from `myStack` into `helper`; the order is now upside down.
`myStack` is empty, so `myStack.push(x)` makes `x` the bottom.
Pop everything from `helper` back onto `myStack`; reversing twice restores the original order.
Return `myStack`.
files.input_note: The number of test cases; each case is `n x`, then the n stack values from bottom to top.
files.output_note: `bottom -> top: 9 7 1 4 5` and `bottom -> top: 2 8`: `x` is at the bottom and the other values keep their order.

check.q: Why does pouring through `helper` twice not scramble the order?
check.a: Each pour reverses the order once, and two reversals cancel out.

files.title: Maximum equal stack sum
files.what: Keeps popping the top of whichever stack has the largest sum until the three sums are equal. Popping only makes sums smaller, so the first time they meet is the largest equal sum.
steps: `stackSum` adds up a copy of a stack (taken by value so the real stack is untouched).
Store the three sums in `sum1`, `sum2`, `sum3` once.
While they are not all equal, find the largest sum, subtract its stack's `top()` and `pop()` it.
When all three match, return `sum1`. If stacks run empty, the sums meet at 0.
files.complexity: Time O(n1 + n2 + n3) · Space O(1) extra (plus the copies made by `stackSum`)
files.input_note: The number of test cases; each case has three lines, one per stack: its size, then its values from the TOP down.
files.output_note: `maxSum = 5` for the first case: sums 8, 9, 7 shrink to 5, 5, 5 after removing 3; 4; and 1, 1. `maxSum = 0` for the second case: three single values that never match, so all of them go.
files.watch_out: The driver pushes each line in reverse so that the first value read ends on top. If you type the values bottom-first instead, the answer changes.

check.q: Why is it always the stack with the largest sum that loses its top?
check.a: The other stacks can only get smaller, so they can never climb up to the largest sum; that stack has to come down.

files.title: Reverse a queue with a stack
files.what: Pours the queue into a stack and back again. The queue keeps order and the stack flips it, so the values come back reversed.
steps: Move every value from the front of `q` onto the stack `st`.
The old back of the queue is now on top of the stack.
Move every value from `st` back into `q`; the old back re-enters first and becomes the new front.
Return `q`.
files.input_note: The number of test cases; each case is n, then the n values from front to back.
files.output_note: `9` (one value is its own reverse) and `3 12 8 6 10`, printed front to back.

check.q: Could you reverse a queue using only another queue?
check.a: Not in the same simple way: a queue returns values in the order they went in, so pouring into a queue copies the order instead of flipping it.

files.title: Min Stack with a second stack of minimums
files.what: Keeps a second stack `mins` beside the real one. At every level it stores the smallest value so far, so `getMin()` just reads its top in O(1).
steps: `push(val)` pushes `val` on `st` and pushes `min(val, mins.top())` on `mins` (just `val` when `mins` is empty).
`pop()` pops both stacks, so they always have the same height.
`top()` returns `st.top()`.
`getMin()` returns `mins.top()`, the minimum saved for the current height.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input:
9
push -2
push 0
push -3
getMin
pop
top
getMin
push -2
getMin
files.input_note: The number of commands, then one command per line: `push x`, `pop`, `top` or `getMin`.
files.output_note: `getMin -> -3`, then after `pop`: `top -> 0` and `getMin -> -2`, exactly LeetCode's example. Pushing -2 again keeps the minimum at -2.
files.watch_out: LeetCode never calls `pop`, `top` or `getMin` on an empty stack, so this class has no empty checks; the Code360 version below must return -1 instead.

check.q: After push 4, push 6, push 1, what does `mins` hold, bottom to top?

files.title: A stack built on a singly linked list

problem.name: Code360 - Implement Stack With Linked List

files.what: Uses the head of a singly linked list as the top of the stack, because a head can be added and removed in O(1). A `size` counter makes `getSize()` O(1) too.
steps: `head` is the top (`NULL` when empty) and `size` counts the nodes.
`push(data)`: the new node's `next` points at the old `head`, then it becomes `head`; `size++`.
`pop()`: return at once if empty; otherwise move `head` to `head->next`, `delete` the old node, `size--`.
`getTop()` returns `head->data`, or -1 when the stack is empty.
`isEmpty()` is `size == 0`.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input:
9
push 4
push 8
top
size
pop
top
pop
isEmpty
top
files.input_note: The number of commands, then one per line: `push x`, `pop`, `top`, `size` or `isEmpty`.
files.output_note: `top -> 8` and `size -> 2` after two pushes; after one pop `top -> 4`; after the second pop `isEmpty -> true` and `top -> -1`, the judge's value for an empty stack.
files.watch_out: Putting the top at the tail instead would make `pop` O(n), because a singly list cannot step back from the tail to the node before it.

check.q: Why is the head, not the tail, the top of this stack?
check.a: Adding and removing at the head are both O(1) in a singly linked list; removing the tail needs the node before it, which means walking the list.

files.title: A queue built on a singly linked list

problem.name: Code360 - Queue Using Array or Singly Linked List

files.what: Keeps `head` as the front and `tail` as the back of a singly linked list, so `enqueue` (at the tail) and `dequeue` (at the head) are both O(1).
steps: `enqueue(data)`: in an empty queue the new node is both `head` and `tail`; otherwise hook it after `tail` and move `tail` to it.
`dequeue()`: return -1 if empty; otherwise save `head->data`, move `head` forward and delete the old node.
If that emptied the queue, set `tail = NULL` too.
`front()` returns `head->data`, or -1 when empty; `isEmpty()` checks `head == NULL`.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input:
9
enqueue 10
enqueue 20
front
dequeue
dequeue
isEmpty
dequeue
enqueue 30
front
files.input_note: The number of commands, then one per line: `enqueue x`, `dequeue`, `front` or `isEmpty`.
files.output_note: `front -> 10`, then `dequeue -> 10` and `dequeue -> 20` (first in, first out), `isEmpty -> true`, `dequeue -> -1` on the empty queue, and after `enqueue 30` the front is 30.
files.watch_out: Forgetting `tail = NULL` when the last node is removed leaves `tail` pointing at freed memory; the next `enqueue` would then write into it instead of starting a new list.

check.q: Why does the class keep a `tail` pointer at all?
check.a: Without it, every `enqueue` would walk the whole list to find the last node, which is O(n).

files.title: Reverse the first k elements of a queue

problem.name: Code360 - Reverse First K Elements of Queue

files.what: Pops the first k values into a stack, pushes them back (now reversed, at the back), then rotates the other n - k values once so they end up behind the reversed block.
steps: Save `n = q.size()` before anything moves.
Pop the first `k` values from `q` and push them on `st`.
Pop `st` back into `q`: the reversed block joins at the back.
Rotate `n - k` times (`q.push(q.front()); q.pop();`) so the untouched values move behind the block in their own order.
Return `q`.
files.input_note: The number of test cases; each case is `n k`, then the n values from front to back.
files.output_note: `3 2 1 4 5` and `40 30 20 10` (with k = n the whole queue is reversed and no rotation is needed).
files.watch_out: Using `q.size()` inside the rotation loop would be wrong, because the size you want is the original n, and it is safer to save it once at the start.

check.q: For `1 2 3 4 5` and k = 2, what does the queue look like after phase 2, before rotating?

files.title: Min Stack that answers -1 when empty
files.what: A min stack where `mins` only records a value when it is a new minimum or ties the current one, and every empty-stack call returns -1.
steps: `push(num)` always pushes on `st`, and also on `mins` when `mins` is empty or `num <= mins.top()`.
`pop()` returns -1 when empty; otherwise it pops `st`, and if the popped value equals `mins.top()` it pops `mins` too.
`top()` returns `st.top()` or -1.
`getMin()` returns `mins.top()` or -1.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input:
10
push 5
push 3
push 3
push 7
getMin
pop
pop
getMin
pop
getMin
files.input_note: The number of commands, then one per line: `push x`, `pop`, `top` or `getMin`.
files.output_note: `getMin -> 3`, `pop -> 7` (7 never went into `mins`), `pop -> 3`, `getMin -> 3` because the second 3 is still recorded, then `pop -> 3` and `getMin -> 5`.
files.watch_out: The comparison must be `<=`, not `<`: with `<` only one of the two 3s is recorded, and popping the first 3 would wrongly report 5 as the minimum.

check.q: Pushing 8, 9, 10 in that order: how many values does `mins` hold?
check.a: Just one, 8: 9 and 10 are bigger than the minimum, so they are never recorded.

files.title: Kevin's stack problem: reverse a string
files.what: Reverses a string by pushing every character on a stack and popping them all into the answer.
steps: Push each character of `s` from left to right; the last one ends on top.
Pop until the stack is empty, appending each `top()` to `ans`.
The last character comes out first, so `ans` is `s` reversed.
files.input_note: The number of test cases, then one string per line.

check.q: What is the reverse of `level`, and what does that tell you about the word?
check.a: `level` again: the word is a palindrome.

practice_links.name: Reverse First K Elements of Queue

recap: Newest-first or 'cancel the last thing' problems are stack problems.
Arrival-order or rotation problems are queue problems.
A stack reverses order; use that to reverse a queue or part of it.
A second stack of running minimums gives O(1) `getMin`.

check_yourself.q: For the string `([)]`, at which character does the bracket check fail, and why?
check_yourself.a: At `)`: the top of the stack is `[`, which is not the partner of `)`.

check_yourself.q: Why is a string like `((` invalid even though no mismatch happens?
check_yourself.a: Because the stack is not empty at the end; two brackets were never closed.

check_yourself.q: You push 5, 3, 7 into a min stack. What does the helper stack hold, bottom to top?
check_yourself.a: 5, 3, 3 — each level stores the smallest value seen so far.

check_yourself.q: How do you reverse only the first k items of a queue of size n?
check_yourself.a: Pop k items into a stack, push them back into the queue (now reversed at the back), then move the front n-k items to the back once each.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: reversing the first 3 of `1 2 3 4 5`
body: The second worked example above, step by step. The queue is drawn front-first, the stack bottom-first, so the end each structure is used at is marked with a `^`.
There are three separate phases and it helps to name them as they go past: pour the first three into a stack, pour the stack back, then rotate the untouched values round to the back.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows or Play to follow all three phases

frames.label: The queue holds `1 2 3 4 5`. Only the first three must be reversed; 4 and 5 have to end up behind them, still in their own order.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  1 2 3 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Phase one. Take the front value off the queue and push it on the stack. 1 leaves the queue, 1 lands on the stack.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  2 3 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1
                      ^ top

frames.label: Take 2 the same way. It goes **on top of** 1, which is the whole point - the stack is storing them upside down.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  3 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1 2
                        ^ top

frames.label: And 3. The first three values are now all on the stack with 3 on top, and the queue holds only the part we must not disturb.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1 2 3
                          ^ top

frames.label: Phase two: pour the stack back. `top()` is 3, so 3 is the first one to rejoin the queue - and it joins at the **back**, behind 4 and 5.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5 3
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1 2
                        ^ top

frames.label: Then 2, which is now the top.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5 3 2
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1
                      ^ top

frames.label: Then 1 last of all. The first three are reversed - but they are sitting at the back of the line, which is not where they belong.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5 3 2 1
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Phase three: rotate. Pop the front value 4 and push it straight back on. Nothing is lost; the line just turns round by one place.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  5 3 2 1 4
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Rotate the second untouched value, 5, the same way, and it is done: `3 2 1 4 5`. The number of rotations is `n - k`, here 5 - 3 = 2, which is exactly how many values were never meant to move.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  3 2 1 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: cancelling the pairs in `abbaca`
body: The same stack, a different question: remove every pair of equal letters that stand next to each other, and keep going while removing one pair creates another.
The rule in the snippet above is the whole program: if the new letter equals the top of the stack, pop instead of pushing. Watch the stack hold the letters that have survived so far.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to read the word one letter at a time

frames.label: Reading `abbaca` left to right. The stack will hold every letter that has not been cancelled yet, in order, so its top is always the letter immediately to the left of where we are.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a


stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Read `a`. The stack is empty, so there is nothing for it to cancel with. Push it.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
          ^ push

stack bottom -> top:  a

frames.label: Read `b`. The top is `a`, which is different, so this is not a pair. Push `b` on top.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
            ^ top is a - different, push

stack bottom -> top:  a b
                        ^ top

frames.label: Read the second `b`. The top **is** `b`, so these two are a neighbouring pair: pop the top and do not push the new one. Both are gone at once.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
              ^ top was b - pop, both go

stack bottom -> top:  a

frames.label: Read `a`. Removing the two b's has made this `a` a neighbour of the first `a`, and the stack already knew: its top is `a`. Pop, and that pair goes too.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
                ^ top was a - pop, both go

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Read `c`. The stack is empty again, so `c` has no neighbour on its left. Push it.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
                  ^ push

stack bottom -> top:  c

frames.label: Read the last `a`. The top is `c`, which is different, so push. Nothing left to cancel.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
                    ^ top is c - different, push

stack bottom -> top:  c a
                        ^ top

frames.label: The word is finished, so read the stack from the bottom up: `ca`. Every letter was pushed at most once and popped at most once, so one single pass does the whole job - and the stack found the chain reaction in the middle without ever looking backwards.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a


stack bottom -> top:  c a
                        ^ top
